text: Lemonade is the sixth studio album by American singer and songwriter Beyoncé, surprise-released on April 23, 2016, by Parkwood Entertainment and Columbia Records, as a visual album paired with a film of the same name. It is conceived as a concept album that explores the historical Black female experience in the United States, allegorized as a personal journey through marital betrayal and healing, and structured as a song cycle based on the Kübler-Ross model. Categorized by critics as an eclectic, genre-blending album with avant-garde and art pop elements, Lemonade incorporates a wide range of genres including R&B, rock, country, soul, blues, hip-hop, jazz, reggae, pop, gospel, and funk. The album features guest vocals from Jack White, the Weeknd, James Blake, and Kendrick Lamar. Upon release, it topped the charts and received platinum certifications in several countries across Europe, the Americas, and Asia–Pacific, becoming the world's best-selling album of the year. It was supported by five singles and promoted through a series of televized performances and the Formation World Tour—the first all-stadium tour by a female artist. Lemonade was hailed as an instant classic and has since been named one of the greatest albums of all time, receiving praise for its experimental post-genre production, nuanced vocal performance, and political subject matter reflecting Beyoncé's personal life. It was music critics' top album of 2016 according to the BBC, named the greatest album of the 2010s by the Associated Press, and topped Rolling Stone's Greatest Albums of the 21st Century list. One of the most Grammy-nominated albums in history, Lemonade won Best Urban Contemporary Album and Best Music Video at the 59th Grammy Awards and also won a Peabody Award in Entertainment at the 76th Annual Peabody Awards, receiving four nominations at the 68th Primetime Emmy Awards. The album is considered a cultural phenomenon, sparking widespread discourse on its personal revelations and socio-political commentary, influencing the entertainment industry, inspiring other musicians and visual artists, and igniting trends across music, fashion, and pop culture. It has also been the subject of extensive analysis in academic journals, college courses, books, and museum exhibitions. Beyoncé's career transformed with the release of her fifth studio album, Beyoncé (2013), which received widespread commercial and critical success and influenced how music is released in the digital age, elevating her from a leading pop star to an auteur who defied industry conventions. The following year, her personal life became a subject of public scrutiny after rumors of Jay-Z's infidelity spread, fueled by leaked elevator footage at the 2014 Met Gala showing Beyoncé's sister Solange physically attacking Jay-Z. The family released a joint statement to assuage concerns, and although divorce rumors continued during their joint On The Run Tour (2014), the couple presented a unified front. On February 6, 2016, Beyoncé released "Formation" as a free download via Tidal, accompanied by an unlisted music video on YouTube. The track, blending trap and bounce, celebrated her culture, identity, and success as a Black woman from the Southern United States. The song and video were met with widespread acclaim, with critics praising it as a personal and political ode to Black Southern heritage. Beyoncé performed the song a day after its release during the Super Bowl 50 halftime show, and a commercial aired afterward announcing the Formation World Tour, with pre-sales opening two days later. The performance received rave reviews from fans and critics but was met with backlash, boycotts, and protests from some conservative figures and law enforcement organizations over perceived anti-police, anti-American, and anti-white racist messages. In an interview with Elle published on April 4, 2016, Beyoncé stated her desire to create art that promotes healing and transformation, saying: "I hope I can create art that helps people heal. Art that makes people feel proud of their struggle. Everyone experiences pain, but sometimes you need to be uncomfortable to transform. Pain is not pretty, but I wasn't able to hold my daughter in my arms until I experienced the pain of childbirth!" Lemonade was recorded between June 2014 and July 2015 across 11 studios in the United States. Beyoncé conceived the idea of writing each song to correspond to a specific emotion forming the chapters of the album and film, and posted mood boards around the studio to guide her collaborators. She and her team played music in the studio to inspire each other. The album was written in stages, with Beyoncé retreating to her home to work with recording and mixing engineer Stuart White and to care for her daughter. The process began at the Record Plant in Los Angeles for a month, followed by a break and a 45-day stay in Paris, where the team stayed in a hotel and set up two studios in separate rooms—one for Beyoncé and one for Jay-Z. Jay-Z described recording as "using our art almost like a therapy session" after his infidelity, and the music Beyoncé recorded separately became Lemonade and was released first. The album was produced through Beyoncé's synthesis of many collaborators, including both popular and lesser-known artists. Beyoncé oversaw all aspects of the writing and production process; co-writers MNEK and Jonny Coffer noted she had a clear vision for how the songs should sound, consistently offering direction and suggestions. The songs were developed piecemeal, with Beyoncé combining material she wrote herself with elements from other writers. Collaborator MeLo-X described her production style as highly distinctive, saying: "She has a way of creating that I've never seen before as an artist. She produces, alters and arranges tracks in ways I wouldn't think of." As a multimedia audiovisual artwork, Lemonade relates the emotional journey of Beyoncé after Jay-Z's infidelity in a generational and racial context through its music, lyrics, visuals, and poetry. The album is a song cycle referencing the classical compositional genre defined by Robert Schumann, Franz Schubert, and Johannes Brahms, with the tracks (excluding "Formation") corresponding to the eleven chapters of the Lemonade film: "Intuition", "Denial", "Anger", "Apathy", "Emptiness", "Accountability", "Reformation", "Forgiveness", "Resurrection", "Hope", and "Redemption." Melina Matsoukas, director of the "Formation" music video, stated that Beyoncé explained the concept behind Lemonade, saying she wanted to show the historical impact of slavery on Black love and how Black families, men, and women are socially conditioned not to be together. In a 2018 Vogue article, Beyoncé wrote about "generational curses" in her family, including a slave owner who married a slave, and explained that only after seeing this clearly was she able to resolve conflicts in her own relationship. She wrote: "Connecting to the past and knowing our history makes us both bruised and beautiful." This theme is repeated throughout Lemonade, with Beyoncé's grief, trauma, and struggle connected to that of her ancestors. The sixth track, "Daddy Lessons," acts as a turning point, linking Jay-Z cheating on her with her father Mathew Knowles cheating on her mother Tina. Towards the end of Lemonade, Beyoncé reveals the meaning behind the title, showing Jay-Z's grandmother Hattie White saying: "I had my ups and downs, but I always find the inner strength to pull myself up. I was served lemons, but I made lemonade," and describing her own grandmother, Agnez Deréon, as an "alchemist" who "spun gold out of this hard life" with instructions passed down through generations like a lemonade recipe. Miriam Bale for Billboard called Lemonade "a revolutionary work of Black feminism" as "a movie made by a black woman, starring Black women, and for Black women," in which Beyoncé is seen gathering, uniting, and leading Black women throughout the film. The album also chronicles the relationship between Black women and American society, including how the United States betrayed and continually mistreats Black women, with society needing to solve its problems to enable reformation and rehabilitation. Lemonade centralizes the experiences of Black women in a way rarely seen in media, celebrating their achievements despite adversity. "Don't Hurt Yourself" contains a quote from Malcolm X: "The most disrespected person in America is the Black woman. The most unprotected person in America is the Black woman. The most neglected person in America is the Black woman." The film features Black female public figures with successful careers despite facing misogynoir and racism, and includes clips of everyday Black women from working-class communities, bringing visibility to those often ignored. The film envisions a space where there was never oppression of Black women, with Beyoncé and other Black women forming a self-sufficient community to heal together. Lemonade defies and dismantles stereotypical representations of Black women as monolithic and angry, instead attributing them complexity, agency, strength, and vulnerability. To create Lemonade, Beyoncé drew from the work of many Black women often overlooked or forgotten. The music draws inspiration from Black female blues musicians such as Shug Avery, Bessie Smith, and Sister Rosetta Tharpe, who used personal trauma to empower Black women, as well as samples songs originally recorded by Black women like Memphis Minnie and Dionne Warwick, whose most famous recordings were by male or white artists. These musical references situate Lemonade within the broader tradition of blues women who used their art to voice Black women's emotional experiences and social realities. The visuals draw inspiration from Black feminists such as Julie Dash's Daughters Of The Dust, Alice Walker's In Search Of Our Mothers' Gardens, and Toni Morrison's The Bluest Eye. Other influences include literary works by Black women focusing on African-American folklore (such as Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God) and Afrofuturism (such as Octavia Butler's Kindred). Beyoncé specifically moves away from her typical music roots to develop a more communal spotlight on artistic hoodoo with other Black female creatives. Beyoncé also uses Lemonade as a form of recognition, commemoration, and celebration of the culture and history of Black people in the Deep South and the United States as a whole. The film contains allusions to slavery, such as the House of Slaves' Door of No Return in Senegal and the dungeons of Elmina Castle in Ghana, where slaves were taken before being shipped to the Americas. In "Love Drought," Beyoncé walks with her dancers into the sea, alluding to the Igbo Landing of 1803, where Igbo slaves took control of their slave ship and marched into the sea while singing in Igbo, drowning themselves. Beyoncé appears wearing a tignon, referencing Louisiana's tignon laws implemented in 1786 that limited African-American women's dress to maintain racist social hierarchies. The film includes references to African religion and spirituality, such as Yoruba ori body paint in "Sorry," allusions to the loa Erzulie Red-Eyes in "Don't Hurt Yourself," and Beyoncé's initiation into the Santería religion and embodiment of the Yoruba orisha Oshun in "Hold Up." Allusions to New Orleans culture include "Queen of Creole cuisine" Leah Chase, the Edna Karr Marching Band, jazz funerals, Mardi Gras Indians, and the Superdome. In Lemonade, Beyoncé is seen with other Black women on plantations. In the "Formation" video, the walls of plantation houses are covered with French Renaissance-style portraits of Black subjects; director Melina Matsoukas stated that "films about slavery traditionally feature white people in these roles of power and position. I wanted to turn those images on their head." Towards the end of Lemonade, Beyoncé and several Black women are on a plantation, with Chris Kelly for Fact writing that "Instead of an antebellum memory, these scenes portray a dream: the fantasy of an all-Black, matriarchal utopia when women dress up, prepare meals, take photographs, and perform shows, not for a master but for themselves." Throughout the film, Beyoncé can be seen in Fort Macomb, a Confederate States Army stronghold taken over by the 1st Louisiana Native Guard, eventually destroyed by Hurricane Katrina. On "Daddy Lessons," Beyoncé is seen standing in a hideaway in the fort, alluding to the Underground Railroad. However, on the closer "All Night," Beyoncé is seen above ground, walking on top of the ruins of the fort in an antebellum-style dress made in West African material, possibly inspired by artist Yinka Shonibare, known for reappropriating "European import — the cloth — to remake symbols of European cultural dominance in the spirit of Africa." On "Don't Hurt Yourself," Beyoncé samples Led Zeppelin's "When the Levee Breaks," originally written by Black Delta blues artists Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie, referring to the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 that displaced hundreds of thousands of African Americans. With this sample, Beyoncé reappropriates a song written by Black people about Black history. In general, she reappropriates genres influenced by African Americans that are now seen as predominantly white, such as rock in "Don't Hurt Yourself" and country in "Daddy Lessons." Lemonade is an eclectic, genre-blending album that explores many musical styles. Vox's Alissa Wilkinson described it as an R&B-rock-country-soul album, with other genres including blues, hip-hop, jazz, reggae, pop, gospel, and funk. The Nation's Erin Vanderhoof characterized it as avant-garde, while Pitchfork's Marc Hogan called it an art pop album. Kariann Goldschmitt, music lecturer at the University of Cambridge, described the album's experimentation with musical styles as a "recuperative historiography" of African-American contributions to diverse genres of music. The album features musicians Jack White, Kendrick Lamar, and bassist Marcus Miller, and samples folk music collected by John Lomax, Sr. and his son Alan Lomax on "Freedom." Beyoncé and her team reference the musical memories of all those periods, including a brass band, stomping blues rock, ultraslow avant-R&B, preaching, a prison song (both collected by John and Alan Lomax), and the sound of 1960s fuzz-tone guitar psychedelia (sampling the Puerto Rican band Kaleidoscope). The Washington Post called the album a "surprisingly furious song cycle about infidelity and revenge." The Chicago Tribune described it as not just a mere grab for popular music dominance, but a retrospective allowing the listener to explore Beyoncé's personal circumstances, with musical tones from the southern United States, harking back to her formative years in Texas. AllMusic wrote that Beyoncé "delights in her Blackness, femininity, and Southern origin with supreme wordplay." On the album, Isaac Hayes and Andy Williams are among the sampled artists. PopMatters noticed the album's nuanced theme of anger and betrayal with vast swathes of political context, though it remains a pop album at its essence with darker and praiseworthy tones. There are two suggested inspirations for the title. The song "Freedom" ends with an audio recording of Hattie White, grandmother of Beyoncé's husband Jay-Z, telling a crowd at her ninetieth birthday party in December 2015: "I had my ups and downs, but I always find the inner strength to pull myself up. I was served lemons, but I made lemonade."

Lemonade is a surprisingly furious song cycle about infidelity and revenge, described by the Chicago Tribune as more than a mere attempt to dominate popular music, instead serving as a retrospective that allows listeners to explore Beyoncé's personal circumstances, with musical tones reflecting her formative years in Texas. AllMusic praised Beyoncé for "delighting in her Blackness, femininity, and Southern origin with supreme wordplay," and noted that the album samples artists such as Isaac Hayes and Andy Williams. PopMatters highlighted the album's nuanced exploration of anger and betrayal, embedded with political context, while acknowledging its fundamental pop essence and darker, praiseworthy tones. The title is linked to two inspirations: the song "Freedom" ends with an audio clip of Hattie White, grandmother of Jay-Z, at her 90th birthday party in December 2015, reciting, "I was served lemons, but I made lemonade," a reference to the proverb encouraging turning difficulty into something positive; Beyoncé also draws on her own grandmother Agnez Deréon’s lemonade recipe as a metaphor for intergenerational healing. The album’s cover, taken from the "Don't Hurt Yourself" music video, features Beyoncé in cornrows and a fur coat, leaning against a Chevrolet Suburban and covering her face with her arm, noted for its stark, minimalist style that reflects the album’s raw emotional themes. In 2023, Joe Lynch of Billboard ranked it the 99th best album cover of all time. Lemonade was first released for online streaming via Tidal on April 23, 2016, through Parkwood Entertainment and Columbia Records, with a digital download the following day, and was released on CD and DVD on May 6, 2016. A limited edition box set titled How to Make Lemonade was available for pre-order on August 18, 2017, including a six-hundred-page coffee table book with behind-the-scenes content and a double vinyl LP; standalone vinyl followed on September 15, 2017. Initially exclusive to Tidal, the album was added to other streaming platforms on April 23, 2019, exactly three years after release, with the version including the original audio and the original demo of "Sorry" as a bonus. Beyoncé aimed to perform the entire Lemonade album live; she performed "Formation" at the Super Bowl 50 halftime show, which critics lauded and which sparked discussions on political symbolism. At the 2016 BET Awards on June 27, she performed "Freedom" with Kendrick Lamar, beginning with a clip of Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech, and the performance was critically acclaimed. At the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards on August 28, she performed a sixteen-minute medley of "Pray You Catch Me," "Hold Up," "Sorry," "Don't Hurt Yourself," and "Formation," including interludes from the Lemonade film, with critics noting political symbolism such as dancers falling as though shot, alluding to police brutality, and a black man in a black hoodie lifting her, referencing Trayvon Martin. On October 19, she performed "6 Inch" and "All Night" at a TIDAL X benefit concert in Brooklyn; on November 2, she performed "Daddy Lessons" with the Dixie Chicks at the 50th Annual CMA Awards, a performance praised by critics but criticized by conservative country fans, sparking debates about country music and Black presence in it, leading to a remix of "Daddy Lessons" featuring the Dixie Chicks. At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards on February 12, 2017, she performed "Love Drought" and "Sandcastles," a performance themed around motherhood that evoked female deities and Renaissance European Christian art, as well as non-European elements like Fulani facepainting, Ethiopian icons, Byzantine jewelry, and Latin American Baroque painting. To promote Lemonade, Beyoncé launched the Formation World Tour from April to October 2016, featuring Es Devlin’s 'Monolith' stage, a revolving seven-storey box with video walls, fire, and fireworks, which critics hailed as a "visual feast" and "emotional tour de force," winning Tour of the Year at the 2016 American Music Awards, being included in Rolling Stone’s 50 Greatest Concerts of the Last 50 Years, and named the best tour of the decade by Consequence of Sound in 2019. The tour ranked number one and number two on Pollstar’s 2016 mid-year Top 100 Tours chart in North America and worldwide, with a mid-year gross of $137.3 million from 25 shows, and a total gross of $256 million from 49 sold-out shows, ranking number two on the 2016 Year-End Tours chart. The album was accompanied by a sixty-five-minute film of the same title, produced by Good Company and Jonathan Lia, which premiered on HBO on April 23, 2016, logging 787,000 viewers and divided into eleven chapters: "Intuition," "Denial," "Anger," "Apathy," "Emptiness," "Accountability," "Reformation," "Forgiveness," "Resurrection," "Hope," and "Redemption." The film features poetry and prose by Warsan Shire, including "The Unbearable Weight of Staying," "Dear Moon," "How to Wear Your Mother's Lipstick," "Nail Technician as Palm Reader," and "For Women Who Are Difficult to Love." The cast includes Ibeyi, Laolu Senbanjo, Amandla Stenberg, Quvenzhané Wallis, Chloe x Halle, Zendaya, and Serena Williams; in "Forward," the mothers of Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, and Eric Garner are shown holding pictures of their sons. Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s daughter Blue Ivy, as well as Jay-Z’s grandmother Hattie White and Beyoncé’s mother Tina Knowles with her husband Richard Lawson on their wedding day in 2015, appear. The film samples Malcolm X’s speech "Who Taught You to Hate Yourself," featured on "Don't Hurt Yourself." The film appeared on several critics’ lists: Pitchfork ranked it number one on their best music videos of 2016; Sight & Sound placed it at number twenty-six on their best films of 2016; David Ehrlich placed it at number twenty-three on his Best Films of 2016 list; Jen Yamato ranked it number nine on her Top 10 Best Films of 2016 list. In June 2016, Matthew Fulks sued Beyoncé, Sony Music, Columbia Records, and Parkwood Entertainment for allegedly copying visual elements from his film Palinoia for the Lemonade trailer, but the lawsuit was dismissed by New York federal judge Jed S. Rakoff. Lemonade included five singles, three of which became major hits; all twelve songs charted on the US Billboard Hot 100. "Formation" was released as the first single exclusively on Tidal on February 6, 2016, with its music video, and was performed at the Super Bowl 50 halftime show; it peaked at number ten on the Hot 100, with its video uploaded to Vevo in December 2016. "Sorry" was released as the second single on May 3, 2016, to rhythmic adult contemporary radio, peaking at number eleven; its video was uploaded on June 22, 2016. "Hold Up" was released to German and UK contemporary hit radio on May 12, 2016, and to US radio on August 16, 2016, peaking at number thirteen; its video was uploaded on September 4, 2016. "Freedom" and "All Night" were released as the fourth and fifth singles, peaking at number thirty-five and thirty-eight respectively. The album received widespread acclaim, with many calling it an instant classic, masterpiece, and Beyoncé's magnum opus; at Metacritic, it received a weighted average score of 92 based on 33 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim." Greg Tate of Spin called it a "triumph of marketing and musicality, spectacle and song, vision and collaboration," praising its deep engagement with Southern Black feminist culture and its emotional and sonic power. AllMusic writer Andy Kellman described it as "culturally seismic" with "layers of meaning and references," noting its cathartic and wounded moments. Rob Sheffield of Rolling Stone called it an "album of emotional discord and marital meltdown" and described Beyoncé’s voice as her "wildest, rawest vocals ever," comparing it to Aretha Franklin’s Spirit in the Dark and Nina Simone’s Silk and Soul. Ray Rahman of Entertainment Weekly called it a "raw and intensely personal plunge into the heart of marital darkness" and a "feminist blueprint," praising its diversity, which includes rock, blues, country, avant-garde, and Texas twang, with Led Zeppelin and Soulja Boy as bedfellows. Alexis Petridis of The Guardian said the album "feels like a success" and that Beyoncé sounded "genuinely imperious," noting the music’s progression from "Pray You Catch Me" to a "righteous frenzy" on "Don't Hurt Yourself." Jonathan Bernstein of The Daily Telegraph called it her strongest work to date and noted the thin line between love and hate. Nekesa Moody and Mohamad Soliman of The Washington Post described it as "deeply personal, yet a bold social and political statement." Jon Pareles of The New York Times praised Beyoncé’s vocals and her courage in addressing widespread issues, noting the album’s independence from radio formats. Greg Kot of the Chicago Tribune felt the artistic advances were "slight" in contrast to its personal, raw, and relatable aspects, calling it a "clearly conceived" piece with a unifying vision. Everett True of The Independent called it "fiery, insurgent, fiercely proud, sprawling and sharply focused," with Beyoncé picking up the mantles of Prince and Nina Simone. Carl Wilson of Slate described it as "a spectacle to rival Thriller" and a "beautiful and often disturbing kaleidoscope" of poetry, feminism, racial politics, history, mythology, emotional upheaval, family, and romance. Kitty Empire of The Observer praised the celebration of female endurance and pragmatism with warmth, anger, and wit, calling it a rare unification of high art and low. Jillian Mapes of Pitchfork noted the album’s signature cadence and attitude, calling Beyoncé a new kind of post-genre pop star. Annie Zaleski of The A.V. Jillian Mapes of Pitchfork stated that the signature cadence, patois, and attitude on Lemonade reflect Beyoncé's status as a hip-hop pop star, yet she also demonstrates a new kind of post-genre pop star. Annie Zaleski of The A.V. Club called it a "seismic step forward" for Beyoncé as a musician, pushing pop music into "smarter, deeper places." Shahzaib Hussain of Clash described Lemonade as Beyoncé at her most benevolent and unadulterated, celebrating Blackness as a "celebratory beacon" and calling it a "long overdue, cathartic retribution." Sal Cinquemani of Slant Magazine called it her "most lyrically and thematically coherent effort to date." Maura Johnston of Time noted the tracks were "fresh yet instantly familiar" with an "over-the-top but intimate" sound. Jamie Milton of DIY said there is "so much more than an enthralling story" in the album, praising Beyoncé as a "risk-taker breaking new ground, up there with the bravest." Exclaim!'s Erin Lowers wrote, "If you've ever been handed lemons, you need Lemonade," calling it "an album in which millions will find their own struggles reflected back to them, as therapeutic as it is utterly dazzling." Britt Julious of Consequence of Sound described how Lemonade, the visual album, weaves emotional grief into art about the Black woman, drawing on Voudou and Southern Black gothic storytelling, and praised its song cycle structure as representing the grief process with "two dichotomous halves," noting it dismantles cycles of abuse and finds healing, purpose, and greatness. Evan Sawdey of PopMatters felt few albums could be considered "as bold, complex, or resolute as Lemonade," and the BBC's Mark Savage described it as having a "complex narrative arc" that "demands to be heard in one sitting," noting Beyoncé had become an albums artist beyond radio play. At the end of 2016, Lemonade was named the critics' top album of the year by the BBC and ranked number one by the most publications (37) on Metacritic, including Rolling Stone, Billboard, Entertainment Weekly, The Guardian, Digital Spy, The Independent, The Associated Press, The New York Times (Jon Pareles list), Los Angeles Times (Mikael Wood list), Pop Matters, Pretty Much Amazing, Idolator, Stereogum, Complex, Consequence of Sound, Wired, and US Weekly. It was named the best album of the 2010s by Consequence of Sound, The Associated Press, and Spex, and the best music video of the decade by The Daily Beast, as well as one of the best movies of the 2010s by Vox. It was included in the top-five albums of the decade by Rolling Stone, The Independent, New York Post, Billboard, Paste, The A.V. Club, WXPN The Key, Refinery29, Tampa Bay Times, Insider, The Young Folks, Genius, Variety, Uproxx, Noisey, The Independent, and The Wild Honey Pie. In January 2025, Rolling Stone named Lemonade the greatest album of the 21st century. Consequence of Sound named it the second best album of the last 15 years (2007–2022). BBC Radio 4 named it the eighth greatest risk in 21st century art, stating Beyoncé "resisted commercial pressure not to be political" and "let audiences into her personal life as never before." The Guardian listed it at number 25 on their 100 best albums of the 21st century. In 2020, Parade named Lemonade the best music video of all time. In 2017, it was ranked number 6 on NPR's list of the 150 Greatest Albums Made By Women. The Daily Telegraph named it the eighth greatest album of all time in 2025, describing it as a "bold, shapeshifting masterpiece channelling personal turmoil into visionary genre-hopping pop." The Quietus placed it at number 9 on their top 100 albums list. Apple Music ranked it number 10 on their list of the 100 Best Albums ever created. Consequence of Sound named it the 18th greatest album of all time in 2022. It is the 29th best album of all time by Metacritic score. On Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time list, it was placed at number 32, citing its exploration of "the betrayals of American blackness" and "all of the country's music traditions." Paste listed it at number 55 on their list of the 300 Greatest Albums of All Time. Lemonade was nominated for four Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Variety Special and Outstanding Directing for a Variety Special. It received eleven nominations at the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards, including Breakthrough Long Form Video for Lemonade, Video of the Year, Best Pop Video, Best Direction, Best Editing, and Best Cinematography for "Formation," Best Female Video and Best Art Direction for "Hold Up," and Best Choreography for "Sorry" and "Formation," winning eight, including Video of the Year and Breakthrough Long Form Video. At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards, it received three nominations: Album of the Year, Best Urban Contemporary Album, and Best Music Film; "Formation" received three: Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Music Video; "Hold Up" was nominated for Best Pop Solo Performance; "Don't Hurt Yourself" for Best Rock Performance; and "Freedom" for Best Rap/Sung Performance. Beyoncé won two awards: Best Urban Contemporary Album and Best Music Video for "Formation." Lemonade won a Peabody Award in Entertainment, with the board of jurors stating it "adroitly brings together stories about betrayal, renewal, and hope," drawing from Black cultural producers to create a "rich tapestry of poetic innovation," immersing viewers in the "sublime worlds of black women, family, and community," and challenging cultural ideas about women of color. In the United States, Lemonade debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with 653,000 album-equivalent units, 485,000 of which were pure album sales, making it the highest opening-week sales for a female act that year and the first artist in chart history to have their first six studio albums debut at number one. In the same week, Beyoncé became the first female artist to chart twelve or more songs on the US Billboard Hot 100 simultaneously. The album slipped to number two in its second week, selling 321,000 album-equivalent units (196,000 pure sales), and remained at number two in its third week with 201,000 album-equivalent units (153,000 pure sales). It was certified platinum by the RIAA in June 2016 and sold 1,554,000 copies and 2,187,000 album-equivalent units in the United States according to Nielsen's 2016 year-end report. After its April 23, 2019, release on streaming, it returned to the top ten on the Billboard 200 at number nine, with the original demo of "Sorry" debuting at number nineteen on the US R&B Songs. On May 20, 2019, it was certified double platinum (2 million copies) and triple platinum (3 million copies) on June 13, 2019. In Canada, it debuted at number one with 33,000 copies and had sold 138,000 album-equivalent units by the end of 2016, 101,000 of which were pure album sales. In the UK, it debuted at number one with 73,000 copies, with 10,000 equivalent sales (14% of total) from streaming—marking the largest ever for a number-one album since streaming was included—and was certified platinum by the BPI for 300,000 copies on September 9, 2016. All of its tracks debuted in the top hundred of the UK Singles Chart. In Australia, it sold 20,490 digital copies in its first week, debuted at number one, and received a double platinum certification from ARIA in 2023 for 140,000 equivalent units. It peaked at number one in Ireland, Belgium, Croatia, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Scotland, and Sweden, and debuted at number one in Brazil, receiving a platinum certification from Pro-Música Brasil. Lemonade is credited with reviving the album concept in an era dominated by singles and streaming and popularizing the release of albums with accompanying films. Jamieson Cox of The Verge called it "the endpoint of a slow shift toward cohesive, self-centered pop albums," stating it "sets a new standard for pop storytelling at the highest possible scale." Megan Carpentier of The Guardian wrote it "almost revived the album format" as an "immersive, densely textured large-scale work" that must be listened to in full. Myf Warhurst on Double J's "Lunch With Myf" explained that Beyoncé "changed [the album] to a narrative with an arc and a story and you have to listen to the entire thing to get the concept." Katherine Schulten of The New York Times asked, "How do you talk about the ongoing evolution of the music video and the autobiographical album without holding up Lemonade as an exemplar of both forms?" Joe Coscarelli noted that some brand-name acts, including Frank Ocean's Endless and Drake's Please Forgive Me, followed Beyoncé's blueprint with high-concept mini-movies. Other projects inspired by Lemonade include Lonely Island's The Unauthorized Bash Brothers Experience, Thom Yorke's Anima, Sturgill Simpson's Sound & Fury, and Kid Cudi's Entergalactic. Beyoncé's use of various genres on Lemonade is credited with setting the precedent for music to transcend genre, with NPR writing that the album "leads us to this moment where post-genre becomes a thing." The use of genres has also been credited with kickstarting the reclamation of certain genres by Black people. "Daddy Lessons" started a trend of "pop stars toying with American West and Southern aesthetics" and set the precedent for "The Yeehaw Agenda," the trend of reclaiming Black cowboy culture. "Don't Hurt Yourself" is credited with the reclaiming of rock by Black women, with Brittany Spanos of Rolling Stone writing that Beyoncé and her peers are giving rock a "second life – and may be what can save it." Several musicians were inspired by Lemonade: Snoop Dogg named his 2016 album Coolaid after it; Sabrina Carpenter said it inspired her to not limit herself, noting it "really transcended every genre"; Cardi B said her 2025 album Am I the Drama? is "going to have my Lemonade moments"; Fergie was inspired to create a visual counterpart for her 2017 album Double Dutchess; Little Mix cited it as inspiration for their 2016 album Glory Days; Ellie Rowsell of Wolf Alice named it one of her favorite albums and said it helped her "put in more thought to what makes a good album flow"; The-Dream wrote a response titled "Lemon Lean" in his 2018 EP Love You to Death; Victoria Monét cited it as inspiration; Lahna Turner released a visual album entitled Limeade; Matt Palmer created his visual EP Get Lost; Todrick Hall made his 2018 album Straight Outta Oz as a visual album due to Lemonade; and Arrow Benjamin said his 2016 EP W.A.R. (We All Rise) was inspired by Lemonade, as every piece was created from a visual perspective. Ann Powers of NPR said Fiona Apple was influenced by Lemonade when implementing Black musical traditions on her 2020 album Fetch the Bolt Cutters; Jenna Wortham of The New York Times drew a parallel between the two albums as "blueprints for how to take in all that emotion and kind of how to push it back out in a way that's cathartic and constructive"; Dan Weiss of Billboard wrote that Shania Twain's Now "couldn't have existed without" Lemonade, calling it an album that "completely changed the course of breakup album history"; Kadeen Griffiths from Bustle stated Lemonade "paved the way" for Alicia Keys' Here and Solange's A Seat at the Table; and Danielle Koku for The Guardian stated that Lemonade aided the return of African mysticism to music.

Lemonade has had a profound and wide-reaching impact across music, fashion, media, academia, and pop culture. Critics have noted that Fiona Apple was influenced by Lemonade when incorporating black musical traditions into her 2020 album Fetch the Bolt Cutters, while Jenna Wortham described both albums as "blueprints for how to take in all that emotion and kind of how to push it back out in a way that's cathartic and constructive." Dan Weiss of Billboard stated that Shania Twain's Now "couldn't have existed without" Lemonade, calling it an album that "completely changed the course of breakup album history" and highlighted as an example of an artist at their full creative peak. Kadeen Griffiths from Bustle noted that Lemonade "paved the way" for Alicia Keys' Here and Solange's A Seat at the Table, while Danielle Koku for The Guardian said Lemonade aided the return of African mysticism to pop music by "stripping it of its ancient pagan labels." Jay-Z's 2017 album 4:44 is seen as a response to Lemonade, with Jay-Z referencing the line "You better call Becky with the good hair" from Beyoncé's "Sorry" and retorting "Let me alone, Becky" in "Family Feud." At the 59th Annual Grammy Awards in 2017, Adele dedicated her Album of the Year award to Beyoncé, calling her "the artist of my life" and stating that Lemonade was "so monumental," and later claimed in a 2021 Vogue interview that Beyoncé should have won the award instead, saying she went into Beyoncé's dressing room to explain that the Grammys' leadership "don't know what a visual album is" and that the award she received was broken, with her wedging a lemon into it—emphasizing that for women of color, Lemonade was a major acknowledgment of their undermined grief. Stevie Wonder called Lemonade "a great work, a great art piece," and Bono included "Freedom" in his "60 Songs That Saved My Life" project, calling it "a platter I had rarely seen." The album inspired artists in film, television, literature, art, and theatre: Misha Green, creator of Lovecraft Country, said Lemonade influenced the show's score by using poetry as a "score"; Bill Condon, director of Beauty and the Beast, cited the visuals as inspiration for the film. The Royal National Theatre's 2018 production of Antony and Cleopatra featured a costume inspired by Lemonade, with designer Evie Gurney drawing a parallel between Cleopatra and Beyoncé as a woman who reclaimed her narrative. The character of Catherine of Aragon in the musical Six was inspired by "Lemonade-era Beyoncé," and Ellie Kendrick's 2018 play Hole at the Royal Court was described as a "stage version of Beyoncé's Lemonade album" focusing on feminism and historical oppression. Fashion stylist Salvador Camarena designed a room dedicated to Lemonade during Modernism Week, citing its "visually stunning" nature and iconic looks. The young adult anthology A Phoenix First Must Burn, edited by Patrice Caldwell, aims to "evocate Beyoncé's Lemonade for a teen audience," and a 2017 video game titled "Lemonade Rage" was created in homage to Lemonade and the "Hold Up" music video. The cover of Marvel's 2017 America comic book paid homage to the "Formation" music video, with the illustrator stating it was a "parallel" to Beyoncé's work on representation, feminism, and fighting for what's right. Marie Claire named the lemonade drop as one of the most influential pop culture moments of the 2010s. Sales for Warsan Shire's chapbook "Teaching My Mother How to Give Birth" increased by 700 to 800% after being included in the Lemonade film. Beyoncé's mention of Red Lobster in "Formation" increased sales by 33%, leading employees to rename menu items and call it the "Beyoncé Bounce." Designers of costumes from Lemonade, such as Natalia Fedner, who designed Beyoncé's dress for "Hold Up," reported career boosts, including being named a "designer to watch" on Entertainment Tonight. The inclusion of imagery from the 1991 film Daughters of the Dust in Lemonade helped bring the film back to theatres, with director Julie Dash stating it "re-confirmed a lot of things that I know to be true about visual style and visual metaphors" and redefined Creole culture. The popular "Lemonade braids" hairstyle is named after a hairstyle Beyoncé wore in Lemonade. Georgia Murray for Refinery29 credited Beyoncé's yellow dress in "Hold Up" with "kickstarting an obsession with yellow" still seen today. The use of the lemon and bee emojis gained meaning after Lemonade's release, with a Twitter spokesperson stating the lemon emoji "took on a meaning of its own." The MTV Video Music Award for Breakthrough Long Form Video, which Beyoncé won at the 2016 MTV VMAs, was reintroduced after 25 years due to Lemonade. Lemonade was parodied and paid homage to in various media: in an episode of Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt titled "Kimmy's Roommate Lemonades!", character Titus Andromedon parodied "Hold Up," "Sorry," and "All Night," coining the term "Lemonading," which was nominated for two Emmys. The "Hold Up" music video was also parodied in The Simpsons, Making a Scene with James Franco, The Ellen DeGeneres Show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, and The Daily Show. SNL produced two sketches: "The Day Beyoncé Turned Black" after the release of "Formation," and "Melanianade," parodying the "Sorry" video with impersonations of Donald Trump's female aides. In a Late Night with Seth Meyers sketch, female staffers paid homage to the visuals, costumes, songs, and poetry. The Late Late Show with James Corden produced a parody titled "Lemonjames: A Visual Monologue," recreating parts of the Lemonade film. Goldie Hawn and Amy Schumer produced a parody of "Formation." The Season 2 premiere of Crazy Ex-Girlfriend featured a musical number that paid homage to Lemonade, including parodies of "Formation" and "Pray You Catch Me." For Beyoncé's 36th birthday, public figures like Michelle Obama and Serena Williams recreated the costume from the "Formation" video. The first episode of James Acaster's 2020 podcast Perfect Sounds focused on "the genius of Lemonade." Scholars and authors outside the music industry have also engaged with Lemonade: a talk at Seminole State College discussed how Beyoncé embodies the conjure woman as a contemporary revision of Zora Neale Hurston's work. The Museum of Design Atlanta launched "The Lemonade Project," a twelve-month series exploring race, gender, and class. Kinitra Brooks and Kameelah Martin produced "The Lemonade Reader," an educational tool analyzing the album's Afrodiasporic influences, visual aesthetics, narrative of grief and healing, and ethnomusicological reach. University of Texas at Austin professor Omise'eke Tinsley wrote Beyoncé in Formation: Remixing Black Feminism (2018), analyzing the album in relation to Black women's sexuality and gender. University of Albany professor Janell Hobson created a lesson plan based on Lemonade, stating it stimulates discussions on Blackness, womanhood, and feminism. Dissect Podcast dedicated its sixth season to Lemonade, with hosts Cole Cuchna and Titi Shodiya offering interpretative analysis combining music theory, lyricism, and social analysis. In a 2020 New York Times article, actress Kerry Washington called Lemonade a "game changer" visually, musically, and sociopolitically. The release of "Formation" and Beyoncé's Super Bowl 50 halftime performance sparked conversation and controversy due to its "unapologetic Blackness," with articles from the BBC and TheWrap analyzing its significance. Many think pieces, particularly by Black women, have analyzed Lemonade's messages, such as Miriam Bale for Billboard who named it "a revolutionary work of black feminism." Megan Carpentier of The Guardian called it a "pop culture phenomenon," stating no other living musical artist could ignite such broad conversations with a new album. Syreeta McFadden noted that "Formation" depicts archetypal southern Black women in ways rarely seen in popular culture. Melissa Harris-Perry of Time said Beyoncé "publicly embraced explicitly feminist Blackness at a politically risky moment," and Candace McDuffie of Glamour said Lemonade made Beyoncé the cultural zeitgeist, reinforcing that her actions cause global pandemonium. Since its release, Lemonade has spawned a large body of academic literature and studies. The University of Texas at San Antonio offered a course in Fall 2016 titled "Black Women, Beyoncé and Popular Culture," which explored the album as a meditation on contemporary Black womanhood and delved into theoretical, historical, and literary frameworks of Black feminism. The University of Tennessee at Chattanooga hosted a "Lemonade Week" in April 2017 featuring discussions on feminism, theatrical performances, African-American women writers and poets, and choreography tutorials. Harvard University hosted "The Lemon Drop," a discussion exploring the nuances of Lemonade. The University of Arkansas offered a course analyzing Black feminism's influence on Beyoncé and Lemonade. The University of Pennsylvania ran two courses exploring politics, race, and gender through Lemonade. Michigan State University hosted a discussion on Lemonade as part of a series on underrepresented and marginalized communities. Chatham University based a writing class on Lemonade, where students examine their place in power systems. Valdosta State University offered a course unpacking themes in Lemonade, including Black identity, feminism, marital infidelity, sisterhood, and faith. The College of Charleston hosted a discussion by Black feminist scholars on Beyoncé's use of southern landscape, Black women, music, and African-based spirituality. The University of North Georgia offered a class titled "Okay, Ladies, Now Let's Get in Formation: Intersectional Feminism in Beyoncé's Lemonade," exploring the music, lyrics, and visuals.
